1.pericope_label: Woe to the rebellious children, saith the Lord, that take counsel, but not of me; and that cover with a covering, but not of my spirit, that they may add sin to sin: that walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked at my mouth; to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh, and to trust in the shadow of Egypt! Therefore shall the strength of Pharaoh be your shame, and the trust in the shadow of Egypt your confusion

schools.summary: Gill identifies the rebellious as a people who were the children of God by national adoption and outward profession but had turned their backs on him, and surveys the datings on offer, the reign of a northern king who sent to Egypt, the times of a later prophet, another king at the end, and the reign of Ahaz, of which there is no record of any such embassy, settling for the reign of Hezekiah himself as the taunts delivered before the walls of the city show. Calvin begins by conceding the objection, that the reproof might seem excessively severe since weak and oppressed men have a right to ask assistance even from wicked persons, nature itself having implanted the principle that human beings should help one another; but at the source there was no ordinary guilt, since it is wicked obstinacy to despise God’s government and follow one’s own inclinations, and this alliance had been strictly forbidden. Of the two reasons for the prohibition he dwells on the general one, that God did not wish his people corrupted by the superstitions of the nations, since we are gradually infected by the vices of those we live among and are more prone by nature to copy vices than virtues; he offers his own country as an example and traces the same immoderate desire for alliances in the opening of one continent and then another to a foreign power. He allows that we may use the services of men, but only so as to depend on God alone, and observes that the prophet sets Pharaoh over against God because creatures are made to contend with God whenever men place their confidence in them. On the third verse he presses the outcome, that the wicked are not merely disappointed of their hope but are labouring hard after their own ruin, nothing acquired by unlawful methods being able to profit anyone, and notes that the strength of Pharaoh is granted by way of concession, as if to say that what they took for protection will yield them nothing but reproach.

Henry sets the habit before the instance, since when the people were pressed by neighbours on one side they had a way of seeking help from neighbours on the other rather than looking up to God, and here, threatened by the Assyrians, they sought the Egyptians and were taunted with it by the enemy’s own officer. He brings two counts against them: they would not consult God, though they had a ready and certain way of doing it by the appointed means, being so confident in the prudence of their own measures that they thought it needless and were unwilling to put the matter to that test, so that they take counsel among themselves but not of God and cover themselves with a shelter that is not of his Spirit, which will prove too short a covering and a refuge of lies; and they could not confide in God, not thinking it enough to have him on their side but strengthening themselves in the strength of Pharaoh.

Clarke renders the disputed phrase as who pour out a libation, since sacrifice and libation were constantly used in ancient times in the ratifying of covenants, so that a libation stands for a covenant as one Greek word does for the same reason, and notes that the Septuagint supports him by rendering it that they made covenants. In his opening argument for the chapter he reads its later half as typical, holding that unless the fall of the Assyrian army is taken as a type of a far greater overthrow, no possible connection can be imagined between the events of Hezekiah’s reign and the far more glorious displays the prophet goes on to describe. Wesley identifies the rebellious as the Jews, glosses the covering as a protection God never required and the asking as enquiry by priests or prophets, and adds that to all their other sins they thus add a distrust of God’s power and mercy and a confidence in an arm of flesh.

Ellicott hears the opening interjection as expressing sorrow rather than indignation, and reads the passage as news, since the intrigues of the palace have at last issued in favour of an alliance with Egypt, an embassy has already been sent, and the thing was done without consulting the recognised prophet; he prefers to render the disputed phrase that weave a web, a term as fit then as now for the subtle intricacies of a double-dealing diplomacy, while reporting a third rendering that they form a molten image, meant not of actual idolatry but of trust in human plans, and notes that the strength of Pharaoh is literally his fortress, used as a symbol of his kingdom. Keil and Delitzsch mark a structural oddity, that the address is barely under way when a heading appears of the same kind as those in the cycle of prophecies against the heathen nations, which several critics dispose of by pronouncing it spurious.

debates: What does the covering mean? Clarke reads a poured libation and so a ratified covenant, with the Septuagint behind him; Ellicott prefers the weaving of a web, a figure for double-dealing diplomacy, and reports a third rendering, the forming of a molten image; Wesley and Henry keep it a shelter sought without God.

When was the embassy sent? Gill canvasses four datings and settles on the reign of Hezekiah, arguing from the taunts delivered before the walls; Ellicott takes the prophecy as news of an embassy already gone, sent without consulting the prophet.

Is it wrong to seek help from a foreign power? Calvin grants that the oppressed may ask help even of wicked men, but holds this alliance forbidden and the guilt to lie in despising God’s government; Henry makes the fault both a refusal to consult God and an inability to trust him.
outliers: Calvin argues that nations catch each other’s vices faster than their virtues, and names his own country as an instance of the damage done by an immoderate appetite for alliances.
Clarke holds that unless the fall of the Assyrian army is read as a type, no connection can be imagined between the events of one reign and the glory the chapter goes on to describe.
Keil and Delitzsch note that a heading of the kind used against foreign nations interrupts the address almost as soon as it begins, and that several critics call it spurious.
themes: a libation, a web, or an image

4.pericope_label: For his princes were at Zoan, and his ambassadors came to Hanes. They were all ashamed of a people that could not profit them, nor be an help nor profit, but a shame, and also a reproach. The burden of the beasts of the south: into the land of trouble and anguish, from whence come the young and old lion, the viper and fiery flying serpent, they will carry their riches upon the shoulders of young asses, and their treasures upon the bunches of camels, to a people that shall not profit them. For the Egyptians shall help in vain, and to no purpose: therefore have I cried concerning this, Their strength is to sit still

schools.summary: Gill takes the princes for those of Judah, sent under the king’s authority, and reports that some take the heading of the sixth verse as beginning a new prophecy and serving as its inscription. Calvin is interested in the cost, since the alliance was bought with long and painful journeys, much toil and vast sums, the envoys arriving loaded with presents at the most distant cities of Egypt, and since those sent were princes and nobles rather than men of ordinary rank the censure is the heavier, for they solicited the alliance slavishly and wandered like suppliants through various countries, when they had no need to go far to seek God, who had invited them by his own promise and assured them they would not call on him in vain there. On the fifth verse he explains that God sometimes bestows prosperity on the wicked in order to punish them more severely, letting them be drawn on by the allurement until they throw themselves down headlong, and distinguishes two ways of failing, since the Egyptians might prove false, as wicked men often forsake at the utmost need those they have fed with empty promises, or might endeavour to the utmost and still be of no use, events being in the hand of God. On the sixth he makes the address to the pack animals a deliberate insult, the prophet turning from men because it was useless to speak to those deaf to every exhortation, and threatening that the effect of the prediction will reach the very beasts though the people do not understand it; the journey was laborious, and their ardour was carried to such a pitch of madness that its tediousness did not discourage them. On the seventh he reads the verse as God’s complaint that his distinct warnings produced no effect, since by sitting still they might have provided for their safety, and takes the crying to mean not words only but chastisement.

Clarke reports that a dozen manuscripts and the Septuagint read the second city name not as a place but as the words in vain, with a matching change in the verb, and gives further variants at the fifth verse. He denies that there is room for a new title at the sixth, takes the word rendered burden in its proper sense as a load rather than an oracle, and asks whether it does not refer to the presents carried south into Egypt; he identifies the country crossed with the same deserts the people had traversed coming out of Egypt, that great and terrible wilderness of fiery serpents and drought, designed as a kind of barrier, of which they had been told they should return no more that way. On the last clause he joins the two final words into a single participle so that the sense becomes Rahab the Inactive, and notes with satisfaction that a learned professor had published the same conjecture independently, a concurrence of different persons adding to its probability. Wesley keeps to the plain sense, the burden being the treasures carried on asses and camels into a land lying south of Judea, and says of the last clause that it were safer and better for them to sit quietly at home, seeking help from God.

Ellicott reads the tenses as the historic present of prophecy rather than as past, and places the two cities, the first among the oldest in Egypt and known to the Greeks under another name, the second identified with a Greek city in the delta of the Nile and among the first the embassy would reach. On the fifth verse he says the prophet paints the dreary disappointment of the embassy, which found Egypt at once weak and false, without the will or the power to help, and he sets beside it the Assyrian officer’s figure of a broken reed that pierces the hand of him who leans on it, together with an Assyrian king’s own record of foes who carried presents seeking alliance with a monarch who could not help them. He records the conjecture that the heading of the sixth verse was a transcriber’s marginal note prompted by the lions, vipers, camels and asses below it, which later found its way into the text, but sees no reason why the prophet should not have prefixed it himself with the sarcasm of an indignant irony, as if to say that they ask for an oracle and shall have one whose very heading implies condemnation and derision. On the last clause he allows that our version fairly gives the meaning, that their boasted strength will prove absolute inaction, but holds that the words as spoken had a more epigrammatic point, Rahab, they are sitting still, the poetical name for Egypt conveying the idea of haughty and inflated arrogance, a phrase that stamps itself on a nation’s memory and is almost a political caricature. Keil and Delitzsch look forward to the command that follows, which is to write the oracle on a table, a separate leaf of durable material, and to do it in the people’s presence so that they might have it before their eyes, noting that the word for book could be used interchangeably since a single completed leaf was so called.

debates: Is the sixth verse a new heading? Gill reports that some take it as beginning a fresh prophecy; Clarke denies there is any room for a new title and reads the word as a load rather than an oracle; Ellicott records the conjecture that a transcriber’s marginal note slipped into the text, but prefers to credit the prophet with an indignant irony.

What does their strength is to sit still mean? Ellicott recovers an epigram, Rahab, they are sitting still, and calls it almost a political caricature; Clarke reaches Rahab the Inactive by joining the last two words into one participle; Calvin and Wesley read it as counsel, that safety lay in staying at home.

Why did the embassy fail? Ellicott says Egypt was at once weak and false; Calvin distinguishes treachery from mere impotence and holds that even an honest effort would have failed, events being in God’s hand.
outliers: Ellicott quotes an Assyrian king’s own record of enemies who carried presents seeking alliance with a monarch who could not help them.
Calvin observes that the envoys crossed deserts and spent fortunes to reach a distant court, when God had promised to be found at home without any journey at all.
Clarke notes that another scholar had independently proposed the same emendation, and takes the agreement of two minds as evidence for it.
themes: a present tense that makes it vivid
treasure on the backs of camels

8.pericope_label: Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever: that this is a rebellious people, lying children, children that will not hear the law of the Lord: which say to the seers, See not; and to the prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things, speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits: get you out of the way, turn aside out of the path, cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us

schools.summary: Calvin supplies the practice behind the command, since it was customary for the prophets to draw up an abridgment of their discourses and attach it to the gates of the temple, and after all had been given time to see and read it the ministers took it down and preserved it among the temple records, which is how the book of the prophets was collected and compiled; when a prediction was remarkable and peculiarly worth remembering, God commanded that it be written in larger characters so that people might be induced to read it more attentively. He draws out the cost to the writer, since there is nothing men resent more strongly than having their crimes made publicly known and fastened on the remembrance of later ages, so that this prophecy must have drawn on its author the intense hatred of all ranks. On the demand made of the prophets he says that wicked men do not merely pour ridicule on doctrine but drive it furiously away and would have it utterly crushed and buried, the power of the word wounding and enraging them until they give vent to their fierceness like wild and savage beasts, from which follow the snares, alarms, persecutions, banishment, tortures and deaths by which they think to root out both the doctrine and the teachers, men being more desirous to have dreams and fabulous tales told them than to be faithfully instructed. He is careful to add that the prophet is not quoting anyone, since these were singularly cunning hypocrites who boasted of worshipping God and complained of being unjustly reproached, and what is given is the state of the fact and their actual dispositions with the mask torn off. He concludes that to set the prophets aside is to set God aside, since God wills to be heard by means of those he charged with declaring his will, so that men who reject the word act as if they denied that he is God. Gill allows the thing written to be either their sins or the prophecy of their destruction and thinks both may be meant, describes the table as wood covered with wax and hung against a wall, and notices that the two clauses of the eleventh verse come to one thing, whether the prophets are asked to leave their usual way of threatening, to get out of the people’s way, or to leave the right way and join them.

Henry gives three reasons for the writing: to shame the men of the present age, who would not hear it spoken, so that their children may profit though they will not; to justify God in the judgments about to fall, since people would think him too severe unless they knew how provoking the nation was and what fair means he had tried before coming to this extremity; and to warn others, even in the remotest place and age, not to do as they did lest they fare as they fared. He notes the care taken over the medium, since it was to be not loose papers which might be lost or torn but a table hung up for public view and a book preserved for posterity, and draws the moral for ministers, that it may be of use not only to preach but to write, since what is written remains.

Clarke prefers for a testimony for ever to for ever and ever, four versions supporting him and two Greek words having dropped out of the remaining copies of the Septuagint. Wesley notes that the thing was to be written twice over, once in a table hung in a public place so that all present might read it and again in a book kept for the use of posterity, and reduces the people’s demand to a sentence, that they would not be troubled with harsh messages from God.

Ellicott takes the command as passing into an act performed before the prophet’s astonished hearers, and reads it as his own sense that what he is about to utter goes beyond the immediate occasion and has a lesson for all time which the world would not willingly let die; but he reports a rival construction, following the Vulgate, which turns the verb into an imperative and gives, they are boasters, cease from them. He identifies the words that follow as those written on the tablet, and explains the people’s motive, that not knowing the law of right themselves they wished the seers to be as blind as they were and would have had the prophets tune their voices to the time; and he hears something particular in the last clause, since the repeated utterance of that one divine title seems to have caused a bitterness of irritation which the more familiar names did not, because it made men feel that they stood face to face with an infinite holiness, and this they could not bear. Keil and Delitzsch insist on translating the demand without varnish, tracing the people’s words back to an unvarnished expression of their true meaning: they forbid the seers to prophesy straight or true things, meaning things not agreeable to their own wishes, and ask instead for what is smooth and insinuating and flattering, and even for illusions or deceits.

debates: Why must it be written as well as spoken? Henry gives three reasons, to shame the present age, to justify God in the coming judgment, and to warn the remotest age; Calvin adds that the prophets kept such abridgments at the temple gates and that weighty predictions were written in larger characters.

Is the opening verb a command to write? Ellicott takes it so and describes the act performed before the hearers, but reports a rival construction following the Latin which makes it an imperative to have done with boasters.

What exactly were the people asking for? Keil and Delitzsch render the demand without varnish, smooth and flattering things and even illusions; Calvin insists these were not spoken words but the actual disposition of cunning hypocrites, exposed by the prophet; Ellicott traces their irritation to the one divine title that would not let them forget an infinite holiness.
outliers: Calvin observes that nothing is resented more than having one’s crimes published and fastened on the memory of later ages, and that the prophecy must have earned its author the hatred of every rank.
Henry draws a lesson for ministers, that it may be of use not only to preach but to write, since what is written remains.
Gill describes the table as wood covered with wax, the writing surface then in use, hung against a wall to be read by all.
themes: a name men could not bear

12.pericope_label: Wherefore thus saith the Holy One of Israel, Because ye despise this word, and trust in oppression and perverseness, and stay thereon: therefore this iniquity shall be to you as a breach ready to fall, swelling out in a high wall, whose breaking cometh suddenly at an instant. And he shall break it as the breaking of the potters’ vessel that is broken in pieces; he shall not spare. For thus saith the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not. But ye said, No; for we will flee upon horses; therefore shall ye flee: and, We will ride upon the swift; therefore shall they that pursue you be swift. One thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one; at the rebuke of five shall ye flee: till ye be left as a beacon upon the top of a mountain, and as an ensign on an hill

schools.summary: Gill notices that the message is introduced with the very title the people had asked to be rid of, and draws a rule from it, that ministers must not seek to please men nor drop a phrase because natural men dislike it, but rather inculcate it the more; he allows the breaking of the vessel to be read impersonally, that it shall be broken. Calvin takes the disputed noun as robbery or the seizing of another’s property, rejects the rendering calumny as too weak, and applies it not to unlawful wealth but to the rebelliousness in which the nation indulged. On the wall he turns the image into a moral, since a wall swells because its parts no longer hold together, so that the haughtiness of wicked men is itself the surest proof that their ruin is near, the more they are puffed up without solid worth the faster they go down by their own weight, men who shake off humility destroying themselves by collecting wind. On the potter’s vessel he observes that a fallen wall leaves stones that can be used again and may even be rebuilt, whereas broken pottery cannot be repaired at all, so that the threat takes away every hope of restoration, which is needed since nothing is harder than rooting a false confidence out of men who have been cast down twice and three times and still raise their crests. He explains why the prophet descends to one instance, since warnings addressed to hypocrites in general terms produce little effect and leave them room to protest that they never rejected the word, whereas by naming the case he strikes their consciences and cuts their sophistry short. On the horses he admires the throwing back of their own confident phrase, since to flee in their mouths meant to escape while in the answer it means to take to flight, so that they shall flee not to find refuge but to turn their backs and be chased by horses swifter than their own; and on the rout he adds that numbers and fortresses avail nothing when the heart fails, no one being strong unless God upholds him by his Spirit.

Clarke proposes reading obliquity for oppression, on a transposition of two letters that he calls a very probable conjecture, and supplies the building practice behind the bulging wall, since the houses of that region are little better than mud walls, one traveller reporting a whole city built of bricks of clay and straw dried in the sun and faced with white plaster, and elsewhere the same bricks with no facing at all, which the least rain dissolves, while another traveller’s note that walls made of earth often cleave from top to bottom he calls exactly apposite. On the rout he argues that a word has dropped out of the second line, which ought to answer to the thousand of the first, and that although the Septuagint supplies many, comparison with two passages in the law shows the true word to be ten thousand. Wesley keeps both senses of the trust, the wealth got by oppression and the perverse course of sending to Egypt, describes the wall as high but bulging in places so that the least accident brings it down, glosses the three terms of the refused remedy in order as returning to God, quieting the mind, and confidence placed on his promises, and says of the end only that it lasts till they be destroyed and few of them left.

Ellicott identifies this word as the prophet’s own message against the alliance and notes that he enforces it as coming from precisely that Holy One of whom they were tired of hearing. He suggests the ill-built and half-decayed houses of Jerusalem furnished the picture of the wall and lays out its three stages, the threatening bulge, then the crack, then the crash, and adds from another prophet the feature of the untempered mortar; he traces the currency of the potter’s vessel to a psalm, notes that a later prophet turns it into an acted parable, and says the schemes were to be not merely crushed but pulverised. Returning and rest he reads as describing a conversion whose particular character the context fixes, a turning from trust in man with all its restless excitement to a trust in God full of calmness and peace. The horses he identifies as the expected Egyptian contingent, on whose fame the generals and statesmen were reckoning, and observes that the prophet, knowing the real temper of Egypt, tells them the animals will serve only for a quicker retreat and not for the charge of battle. On the rout he grants the hyperbole is common enough but points out that an Egyptian king’s own inscription boasts of his strength in the self-same words, which may have given the prophet a special edge of sarcasm; and he corrects the beacon to a pine, finding two of the most striking emblems of solitariness a poet could choose, the tall pine standing alone on a mountain height and the flag-staff seen far off against the sky. Keil and Delitzsch read the same reversal in the verse about the horses and carry it forward into the promise that follows, holding that Israel would have to be reduced to a small remnant before the wrath ceased.

debates: What is the trust that is condemned? Calvin takes the noun for robbery and applies it to rebelliousness rather than to ill-gotten wealth, rejecting the rendering calumny; Clarke would emend it to obliquity; Wesley keeps both the wealth and the embassy.

Where does the image of the wall come from? Clarke supplies the sun-dried brick of the region, which the least rain dissolves; Ellicott points to the half-decayed houses of Jerusalem and names the three stages of collapse; Calvin makes the swelling itself the proof of coming ruin.

What was the point of the horses? Ellicott makes them the expected Egyptian contingent and says they would serve only for a faster retreat; Calvin hears the prophet throwing the people’s own word back at them, since their flight to safety becomes flight from a pursuer.
outliers: Clarke quotes a traveller on cities built entirely of sun-dried clay and straw, which the least rain dissolves, and another on walls of earth cleaving from top to bottom.
Ellicott notes that an Egyptian king’s inscription boasts of his strength in the same words the prophet uses of the rout, which may sharpen the sarcasm.
Ellicott corrects the beacon to a pine and finds two emblems of solitariness, the tall pine on a height and the flag-staff seen alone against the sky.
themes: a title they had asked to be spared
a wall that bulges before it falls

18.pericope_label: And therefore will the Lord wait, that he may be gracious unto you, and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you: for the Lord is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him. For the people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem: thou shalt weep no more: he will be very gracious unto thee at the voice of thy cry; when he shall hear it, he will answer thee

schools.summary: Gill presses the verb of waiting, which he says carries a sense of panting and longing after the moment, and holds that God waits for the worst extremity, when his people have been brought to feel their danger and their sins and to depend on him, so that the mercy is the sweeter when it comes; on the promise he takes the verse as counsel to stay put, abiding in the city and waiting the Lord’s time rather than running to Egypt for shelter. Calvin insists on the word judgment, which he says denotes not punishment only but the moderation exercised in chastening, as when another prophet asks to be chastened in judgment and not in wrath, so that judgment is set against severity, God observing a limit in punishing those whose salvation he is always promoting; he also sets this waiting against the excessive haste rebuked at the chapter’s opening, since the Lord does not render like for like and will not hurry to punish as they hurried to save themselves, and reports without accepting the alternative renderings that God commands them to wait or will cause them to wait. On the promise he thinks it would have seemed incredible after so complete a desolation, yet holds that the Church is preserved, the prophet naming first the mount on which the temple stood and then the city to show that what had been laid waste would be restored and enlarged; and he insists the mourning is not perpetual, since they who sow in tears shall reap in joy, while granting how hard it is to taste any consolation while the mind is overwhelmed by a conviction of God’s vengeance.

Henry reads the turn as an antithesis, that notwithstanding all just threatened the Lord will yet wait, and observes that having shown how those who made Egypt their confidence would be ashamed of it the prophet now shows that those who sat still and made God their confidence would have the comfort of it, which is matter of comfort in bad times since all will be well yet with those that fear God. He glosses the waiting three ways: God waits till they return and seek his face and is then ready to meet them with mercy; he waits so as to give it at the fittest time, when it is most for his glory and comes with the most pleasing surprise; and he continually follows them with favours, letting slip no opportunity of being gracious. On the promise he looks past its nearer fulfilments to the Zion above, where they will weep no more for ever, and adds that even now they would have more comfort, and more holiness, if they were more constant in prayer, and that a famine of bread is not so great a judgment as a famine of the word of God.

Clarke reports a conjecture that reads he shall be silent for he shall be exalted, which one manuscript appears to support while another gives he shall return, and notes that the confusion of two similar letters is a very frequent source of such mistakes. On the promise he argues that a word has fallen out and should be restored from the Septuagint, so that the line reads when a holy people shall dwell in Zion, which clears a sense otherwise extremely obscure, and he recalls that when the other cities of the land were taken by the Assyrian king this one was preserved with all that were in it; he also doubts the negative in the next clause, since the Greek does not acknowledge it and the word may have been written by mistake for another differing only slightly, giving thou shalt implore him with weeping rather than thou shalt weep no more. Wesley compresses the first verse, that God patiently expects their repentance and will work gloriously, glossing judgment as mercy and the waiting as done in his way with faith and patience, and dates the fulfilment of the promise twice over, partly in the return from captivity and more fully in gospel times.

Ellicott puts the thought as a proverb, that man’s extremity is God’s opportunity, and takes the waiting as a longing with eager expectation to come to the rescue, the waiting of the last clause being the same wistful longing on the other side. He would correct two words, since a very slight alteration turns he will be exalted into he will wait in stillness, which suits the context better, while if the received text is kept it must mean that he withdraws himself on high and seems to wait in order to interpose at last effectually; and the God of judgment he would render a God of righteousness. On the promise he observes that the two place-names are practically synonymous and that the prophet lingers on both out of a patriot’s affection, and allows the clause to be read as a vocative. Keil and Delitzsch describe the heirs of the grace that follows the judgment as a people newly pardoned in answer to its own cry for help, led by faithful teachers in the right way, and renouncing its idols with disgust.

debates: What does it mean that God will be exalted? Ellicott would emend to he will wait in stillness and otherwise reads a withdrawal on high before an effectual interposition; Clarke reports manuscripts giving he shall be silent or he shall return; Wesley keeps the received sense, that he will work gloriously.
What is a God of judgment? Calvin makes judgment the moderation exercised in chastening, set against severity; Ellicott would render it righteousness; Wesley glosses it simply as mercy.

Is the promise thou shalt weep no more? Clarke doubts the negative, since the Greek lacks it and a nearly identical word would give thou shalt implore him with weeping; the others keep the received text and read an end of mourning.
outliers: Clarke argues that the word holy has fallen out of the text and can be restored from the Septuagint, clearing an otherwise obscure line.
Gill notes that the verb for waiting carries a sense of panting and longing, and that God waits for the worst extremity so that the mercy may be the sweeter.
Henry remarks that a famine of bread is not so great a judgment as a famine of the word of God.
themes: a holy people restored to the text
weeping, or the end of weeping

20.pericope_label: Though the Lord give you the bread of adversity ... thine ears shall hear a word behind thee ... ye shall defile the covering of thy graven images
debates: Whether the word at the end of the first verse means a teacher or the early rain: Ellicott and Gill take the teachers, Calvin denies that the sense agrees with the context and reads it of food.
Whether the voice behind is conscience, the Spirit, or the written word.
outliers: Clarke reports three old versions rendering the last clause as a prohibition, turn not aside, as though they read a negative for the particle.
themes: The word restored as the chief blessing
Idols profaned as the fruit of repentance

23.pericope_label: Then shall he give the rain of thy seed ... and there shall be upon every high mountain rivers and streams of waters ... the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun
debates: Whether the plenty is literal harvest or an accommodated figure for the blessings of the kingdom: Gill and Wesley take it plainly, Calvin insists it is allegorical.
Whether the comparison to the light of seven days belongs to the text: Clarke calls it a marginal gloss and Keil and Delitzsch report the same verdict widely held, while Calvin and Wesley expound it.
outliers: Clarke emends the falling towers to the falling mighty on the evidence of two old versions and the Chaldee.
themes: Plenty as the fruit of repentance
Light as the measure of the age to come

27.pericope_label: Behold, the name of the Lord cometh from far, burning with his anger ... to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity ... ye shall have a song, as in the night when a holy solemnity is kept
debates: Which feast the song is drawn from: Ellicott argues for the Feast of Tabernacles, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley for the passover.
Whether the name of the Lord is simply God himself, as Gill and Wesley take it, or already carries the weight Ellicott finds in it as an anticipation of later usage.
outliers: Clarke reports an irregular verb form, a proposed redivision of the words, and the judgment that only one ancient version caught the sense of the winnowing image.

30.pericope_label: The Lord shall cause his glorious voice to be heard ... through the voice of the Lord shall the Assyrian be beaten down ... for Tophet is ordained of old
debates: What the grounded staff means: Clarke reports that no one has made tolerable sense of it and prefers a conjectured rod of correction, Ellicott reads the destined rod, Wesley keeps the received word and explains it of God’s fixed purpose.

Whether Tophet names a place of future punishment or a figure for the condition of the wicked: Gill and Clarke trace the name to the valley and to the later word for hell, Calvin denies that any prison is meant.
outliers: Clarke reads against them for against it on the authority of fifty-two manuscripts and five editions.
Ellicott notes the feminine pronoun and that some critics refer it to Jerusalem.
themes: The voice of God as the whole instrument of judgment
The rod that cannot be shaken off
Tophet as the end of the oppressor
